newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: W.African crude shut out of Asia by regional oil.
newsitem.headline: W.African crude shut out of Asia by regional oil.

text.p: West African crude sales to Asia have dropped sharply, shut out by more competitive regional crude prices, traders said on Tuesday.
The last major wave of buying of West African crude -- priced off the North Sea Brent market -- was in early May when buyers secured first half June loadings, the market sources said.
The Brent-Dubai differential is narrow, indicating that economically West African imports are still possible. But traders said the rise in the outright Brent price has left regional prices cheaper.
"The Brent/Dubai spread is still narrow, but Brent is also too high," said a trader. "Economically, regional grades are more attractive."

West African crude deliveries to Asia amounted to some 855,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the first quarter of 1997, five percent higher than the year earlier quarter, London-based tanker broker Simpson, Spence & Young said.
Cabinda was offered at dated Brent -50 cents, they said. The last Cabinda cargo bought by China in early May was heard traded at dated Brent -$1.05.
Refinery maintenance shutdowns in China and South Korea in June and July has also contributed to the lack of demand for West African grades, traders said.
"Maybe when refinery turnarounds are over, and the demand for products heats up, there will be more interest in West African crudes," said a trader.

For the last few weeks buying has slowed. The last big purchases were by China for 4.5 million barrels of West African crudes, including Cabinda, Zafiro, Palanca and Mandji, for loading in the first half of June.
At that time, the price of dated Brent was just above $18.00 per barrel. Dated Brent was valued Tuesday at $19.65.
Despite the rise in Brent, seller's offers of West African cargoes were still too high, further reducing the attractiveness of buying these crudes, traders said.
The switch in crude demand to regional grades has reversed the fortunes of several crudes -- particularly heavy sweet grades -- which have been weak for most of 1997.

In March, Indonesia's heavy-sweet benchmark Minas crude was traded at a discount to its official price, the Indonesian Crude Price (ICP), as China, Japan and South Korea sucked in large volumes of West African oil.
But Minas for June lifting has risen to more than ICP +20 cents, compared to ICP +15 for May cargoes.
The price was expected to rise further, supported by the crude's direct burning qualities as north Asia moves into summer time when air conditioning demand rises.
